title: Early Scottish records
standfirst: The early Scottish records anchor the search for one extended Glasgow family. The next task is to connect its oldest documented households, retaining tentative joins with their evidence and open questions.
question: How can the earliest Glasgow branches be joined into the shared paternal family?
answer: Start with the 1447–1455 Glasgow burgess, the Stirling John of 1475–1480, Alan in the late-fifteenth-century justice record, and the Saltmarket family. The Saltmarket John-to-William property succession is the leading father hypothesis, followed by a proved father–son generation. These working connections guide a single-family reconstruction while the missing identities and generations are tested. The local working tree now selects the Stirling John as an uncertain father of the Saltmarket candidate and, more tentatively, Alan Glasgw. The imported John profile’s identity and Alan’s exact collateral degree remain open.

chapters.title: Issobell: a Mid Calder childhood for the McCaskie bride
body: Select David Glasgow-1028 as the uncertain working father of Issobell Glasgow-3185, the bride indexed with Robert McCaskie at St Cuthbert’s on 19 July 1632, through possible identity with David’s Mid Calder daughter Issobell Glasgow-1085, baptised on 3 May 1612. This adopts an existing comparison in the captured child profile, rather than inventing a new named parent from the marriage alone. Exact forename and surname, the compatible Lothian setting and an age of about twenty in 1632 if baptised near birth favour this childhood as a practical working choice. The child’s baptism names David, but neither it nor the marriage supplies the bridge between child and adult. Shared name and compatible chronology do not prove the identity. Prefer this young-adult explanation provisionally over an older widow or an unrecorded childhood, at low confidence.

Retain Glasgow-1085 and Glasgow-3185 as separate profile accounts of a possible single woman; the selected parent does not establish two distinct daughters called Issobell. The father–daughter link is already confidently marked for the record-defined 1612 child; only the transfer to the 1632 bride is newly selected and uncertain. The marriage index names no father, age, birthplace, prior marital status or children. The 19 July date belongs to a combined banns/marriages index and is not newly verified as the ceremony date. The bride’s before-1612 birth boundary is an inferred profile estimate, not a birth record or an independently established exclusion of the May 1612 child. It is retained unchanged; no new birth date is entered to force the connection. The child’s 1642 Hardington, Somerset death fields remain an unsourced tree-held later-life lead in this review, not a verified fate or proof of migration. Even if correct, that later date alone would not exclude the 1632 marriage. The older Isobel Glasgow-3336, who represents Andrew’s testament-named daughter and is probably the William Symountoun bride of 1619 and mother of the 1620 child, remains a possible remarriage alternative. No death of Symountoun, remarriage record or continuing incompatible household was inspected; do not exclude her merely because she already has a spouse. An unrecorded Isobel remains possible and the candidate list is not exhaustive. No mother is named in the 1612 baptism review, so none is selected for the bride. David’s own selected Andrew-of-Calder father remains uncertain and supplies no independent corroboration. Existing relatives, dates and all confidently marked links are preserved. No identity merge, new original inspection, live WikiTree edit or confidence upgrade is claimed. Working connectivity counts the retained profile accounts, including possible duplicates.

St Cuthbert’s marriage index, 19 July 1632; Issobell and Robert McCaskie; OPR 685/2,20/34,FR337
Captured child profile already compares the 1612 child with the McCaskie bride
Older Isobel and William Symountoun, Edinburgh marriage register p.267 / PDF p.277; retained remarriage alternative

chapters.title: The 1652 Edinburgh cordiner: a working Glasgow childhood
body: Select Robert Glasgow-1027 as the uncertain working father of the Edinburgh cordiner Robert Glasgow-3938 through possible identity with the indexed Glasgow child Robert Glasgow-1078, baptised on 17 November 1618. The published Edinburgh marriage register names Robert as a cordiner with Janet Thomsone on 1 July 1652. The older Robert is the probable identity of the Glasgow cordiner admitted burgess on 22 April 1613 and is the named father of the 1618 child. If baptised near birth, that child would have been about 33 at the July 1652 marriage. The matching name, compatible adult generation and same craft make this a useful preferred family comparison over an otherwise unidentified parent or a more distant cordiner kinsman. The trade association supplies a reason to select the family, but neither hereditary training nor a Glasgow-to-Edinburgh move is documented. The father selection is low confidence; it does not identify the child with the adult as an established fact.

Select Jonet Cunningham-20923 as the independently assessed uncertain mother of the Edinburgh adult only through the same possible childhood identity. The 1618 baptism explicitly names Jonet Conynghame as mother of Robert Glasgow-1078. This is an explicit maternal clause for the child, not an inference from the older Robert’s marriage alone or from a Cunningham surname elsewhere. Its transfer to Glasgow-3938 depends entirely on the uncertain identity and therefore remains uncertain. The father’s craft provides no independent evidence of maternity.

Keep Robert Glasgow-1078, Glasgow-3938 and the Larne Robert Glasgow-3970 as separate profile accounts. Both adult accounts are now provisionally placed in the 1618 child’s family; this does not establish two distinct sons named Robert. The 1652 Edinburgh event and the 1653 Larne account are not simultaneous incompatible events on the available evidence: they could concern one mobile man or different namesakes. Neither a migration nor that combined identity is selected as proved. Robert Glasgow-1149 remains the separate existing candidate for the Euphame Lorimer household. Her indexed children in 1651, 1659, 1662 and 1664 bracket the Thomsone marriage, favouring two Edinburgh men. The reported 1 March 1644 West Port sasine also names Eupham Lorimer and belongs to that household comparison; it does not give a West Port residence or wife to the 1652 bridegroom. The original sasine is uninspected. The 1618 child’s attached younger Cunningham spouse and 1645 James association do not prove his adult identity. A later Thomsone marriage could be a remarriage if that association is correct, but no death or remarriage sequence is supplied. Preserve the existing attachments and all namesake alternatives. Glasgow-3938’s before-1634 birth boundary is an age-derived profile estimate, not a recorded birth. It remains unchanged, as do the child’s baptism, the Larne estimate and all existing spouses, children and confidently marked links. The Edinburgh marriage gives no parents, age or children. No apprentice, burgess, witness, property or migration record joins these accounts. An unrelated cordiner or another son, nephew or cousin in the wider family remains possible. No identity merge, new original inspection, live WikiTree save or relationship-confidence upgrade is claimed. Connectivity counts the retained profile accounts, including possible duplicates.

Glasgow cordiner admission, 22 April 1613; existing reviewed transcription
Glasgow baptism, 17 November 1618, OPR 644/1, reported 10/272; existing transcription names both parents

Reported 1644 West Port sasine index, SRO44 p.160; Lorimer household, original unread

chapters.title: Campbeltown: a provisional Linlithgow origin and Agnes’s placement
body: Select John Glasgow-1561 as the uncertain working father of George Glasgow-3100 of Campbeltown through possible identity with John’s indexed Linlithgow son George-1560 of 20 January 1622. A child baptised in 1622 could have been about 37 at Alexander’s 1659 Campbeltown event and about 28 in the approximate 1650 generation assigned to James and Agnes. This is a workable adult generation for the household. Prefer this comparison provisionally over the older 1605 Mid Calder George-1082, who would have been about 54 in 1659, without excluding that man. The 1627 Glasgow George-1090 is a close alternative, about 32 in 1659; his profile also carries a separate, unproved Fanne Smith household association requiring its own identity review. The preference is weak and practical: the 1622 child has no established incompatible adult fate, and the household timing is compatible. Missing later records are not positive identity evidence. No shared occupation, holding, spouse, witness or migration record identifies the Linlithgow child with the Campbeltown father. This is a very low-confidence family selection, not an identified migration or a record naming the adult’s father.

Select George Glasgow-3100 as Agnes Glasgow-1562’s uncertain working father. This activates the existing geographic family suggestion: Agnes’s captured profile places her Longwill household in Campbeltown, with a 1670 marriage-year field and a son’s 1683 birth field, while George is the named father in the 1659 Campbeltown event. Their approximate parent/child generations permit an older daughter in that household. The same locality and generation make daughter a useful provisional placement alongside George’s attached James and recorded Alexander. The marriage year, child details and Agnes’s circa-1650 birth are profile-held leads, not a newly inspected parish entry. No source names Agnes’s father; a sister, cousin, other local family or unrecorded father remains possible.

George-1560 and George-3100 remain separate profile accounts of a possible single man; shared proposed parentage does not prove two distinct sons called George or an identity merge. The 1605 and 1627 childhood candidates remain viable, and the list is not exhaustive. A separate unrecorded childhood is possible. The illustrative ages assume baptism near birth. George-3100’s 1630 structured and 1640 narrative births are unsupported estimates; neither is silently replaced by a proved 1622 birth. The existing John review cites X1RN-XV7 whereas the child profile cites X1RN-XVQ; retain that reference difference for original-register comparison, without treating the citations as independent events. James-1496’s father link to George is inherited and unproved; its name pattern supplies no independent corroboration for the chosen childhood. Agnes’s 1670 marriage field does not establish her age. No birth year is altered to force a generation. Assess mothers separately. No mother is supplied for the 1622 child in this review and none is selected for the Campbeltown adult. Grizel Dunlop-3562 is already the confidently marked mother of Alexander-3101 in the 1659 event, but that does not establish her maternity of Agnes or James. Her circa-1640 birth is also an unsupported estimate. Neither James nor Agnes receives a mother. The FMP 13 April 1659 birth-date field and Scotland’s People 12 April index date remain literal alternatives; the original entry and reference conventions are unresolved. The Auchinhork residence reading is not assigned a guessed modern place. John-1561’s own Andrew-of-Calder father and his other childhood-to-adult comparisons remain uncertain. No new original inspection, confident relationship upgrade, live WikiTree edit or identity merge is claimed. Connectivity counts profile accounts and retains the possible duplicate.

1659 Campbeltown transcript, Alexander, George and Grizel; literal 13 April birth field
Agnes Glasgow-1562, captured historical profile and family fields; underlying citation unresolved

chapters.title: A provisional Glasgow–Larne–Belfast family
body: Select Robert Glasgow-1027 and Jonet Cunningham-20923 as the uncertain working father and mother of Robert Glaskow of Larne, Glasgow-3970, through the existing possible identity with their son Robert Glasgow-1078, baptised at Glasgow on 17 November 1618. The 1653 Larne account gives no age or parents, and its before-1625 birth boundary permits the 1618 child; that child would have been about 23 during the alleged 1641 events and 35 in 1653. The Scottish child has no established later fate that excludes this adult account. Choose the already recorded possible identity as the working family explanation, at low confidence. The baptism names both parents, so the maternal selection is assessed from that same explicit child clause, not from a Cunningham surname association in Ulster. Both adult parent links depend on the uncertain identity and remain uncertain; the baptism’s direct parentage must not be transferred as proof of the Larne man’s origins.

Select Robert of Larne-3970 as Captain James Glasgow-3172’s uncertain working father. This adopts the existing possible son-or-younger-relative comparison: Larne, Belfast and Kilwaughter form the north-east Antrim setting of the recorded Robert and later James, and an older Robert active in 1641–1653 can precede a shipmaster active by 1667. James commanded the Blessing of Saltcoats in the 1667 Macartney correspondence and the James of Belfast in 1679. These are compatible Scottish-west-coast/Antrim associations, not a parent clause. Son is selected over the unresolved younger-relative alternatives for one provisional paternal route; no mother is selected for James.

Robert-1078 and Robert-3970 remain separate profile accounts of a possible single man; the selected parents do not establish two distinct Robert sons or an identity merge. No record joins the 1618 baptism to Larne, supplies the Larne man’s Scottish origin, or rules out another Robert. The 1666 John of Portrush shipmaster is a further possible identity, not an occupation proved for either Robert; the later Robert/Rachel household remains separate. James-3172, the Scottish child James-3971 of 1645, and the Kilwaughter James-1081 may be one, two or three men. All accounts remain; no identity among those James groups is selected. A child baptised in 1645 could have been a shipmaster aged about 22 in 1667, assuming infant baptism, but that is compatibility only. The father named in that 1645 record is not independently identified with the 1618 child. John-3913’s circa-1630 and Captain James’s circa-1640 births are inherited estimates, not dates that establish or exclude a generation. If John’s 1630 were literal and the Larne man were born in 1618, fatherhood at about twelve would be an important chronological objection; both the age estimate and John’s uncertain paternal attachment require testing. No birth year is changed to force the selected route. Captain James could instead be a nephew, other relative, unrelated namesake, or a member of the Saltcoats sailor John-4152’s family; the named Saltcoats vessel makes that a real competing route, not evidence that John was his father. The two women Cunningham-20923 and Cunningham-22604 are distinct: the elder is the named 1618 mother, the younger the named mother in the 1645 James record. Neither that younger maternity nor a marriage to her is transferred to the Larne adult or captain through these selections. The existing uncertain Kilwaughter father links remain uncertain; none becomes proved by joining their supposed ancestor to Scotland. The Larne allegations are hearsay, not a judicial finding of guilt, and the 1686 will reference is not a proved death date. No new original inspection, certainty upgrade, live WikiTree edit or identity merge is claimed. Connectivity counts profile accounts and does not resolve the possible duplicates.

chapters.title: Jean of Linlithgow: connect the childhood and mother accounts tentatively
body: Select John Glasgow-1561 as the uncertain working father of Jean Glasgow-3083, the mother named in the 1654 Issobell Glen baptism citation. The existing Linlithgow father study places an indexed daughter Jean in John’s household in 1613, represented by Glasgow-3055. The later mother’s profile also places her in Linlithgow. A child baptised in 1613 could have been a mother in 1654, about 41 years later if baptised in infancy. The 1626 birth stated for the later mother has no identified birth source and is not a concrete conflict with that identity. Prefer the possible same-woman explanation and carry the existing father comparison to the adult account, at low confidence. This is a selected inference from the existing local family and chronology, not a parent named in the 1654 citation.

The profiles Glasgow-3055 and Glasgow-3083 remain separate accounts of a possible single woman. The selection establishes neither two distinct daughters called Jean nor a completed identity merge. The 1613 daughter’s later whereabouts are not established. Another Jean in another Glasgow household remains possible; a later daughter in John’s wider family is another explanation. The 1654 citation identifies Jean Glasgow as Issobell Glen’s mother, but its full event fields and original page have not been re-read here. Linlithgow for the adult account comes from her existing profile field, not a newly verified place clause in that baptism. Age 41 assumes baptism near birth and is an illustrative compatibility check, not a recorded maternal age. The 1626 profile year stays an unproved estimate; do not silently replace it with a proved 1613 birth. The saved accounts give 7 and 17 July 1613 and cite both X1RX-HPY and X1RX-HPB; retain these literal differences pending the original register. They are not counted as independent corroborating events. No mother, marriage date, husband’s given name or new child profile is inferred. John’s own selected Andrew-of-Calder father remains uncertain and is not proved by Andrew’s testament. No new original inspection, certain relationship upgrade, live WikiTree edit or identity merge is claimed. Connectivity continues to count profile accounts and therefore does not resolve this possible duplicate.

evidence.label: FamilySearch, Jean Glasgow in Issobell Glen baptism, 1654; existing profile citation
FamilySearch, Jean Glesgow, 1613; Glasgow-3055 source citation
FamilySearch, 1613 daughter in the maintained John-1561 review; day/reference comparison open

chapters.title: Saltcoats: two proved daughters and a possible earlier father
body: The 1637 testament identifies Glasgow-4152 as sailor in Saltcoats, dead December 1636, father of Glasgow-4151 and Glasgow-4153. These father links were already confident; his omitted catalogue page separated the visible family.

Select John Glasgow-3193, the recorded son at Corsankell in 1571 and probable Kilwinning tenant of 1559–60, as the Saltcoats sailor John Glasgow-4152’s uncertain working father. Saltcoats in Ardrossan adjoins the Stevenston–Kilwinning coastal parish cluster where this earlier Glasgow family is documented. A later-sixteenth-century son of the earlier adult could have been a working sailor and father of two daughters by 1636. The choice gives the Saltcoats household a provisional place in an existing local John line, using geography and a feasible generation. It is a low-confidence selection, not a named parent clause or an identification of the two Johns.

No source names the sailor’s parents or age. His former c.1600 birth was an unsupported creation estimate; it is not replaced by an invented older birth to fit this hypothesis. If a birth near 1600 is eventually established, the earlier John would have been an older father, and a grandson or more distant collateral placement could be more natural. Same given name is weak support and does not distinguish this candidate securely from Glasgow-3921 (James younger), another member of the local family, or an unrecorded father. The sailor could belong elsewhere in that family or to another branch. The 1559–60 Kilwinning attribution to the Corsankell John is itself probable, although the 1571 Corsankell family is directly recorded. The same-person alternative is less economical: an adult in 1559 would have been about 95 or older at the sailor’s death in 1636, assuming adulthood at eighteen. That is an illustrative age comparison, not a proved exclusion. The father-versus-grandfather degree remains open. No mother is assigned to the sailor or to his daughters; Agnes Wilson’s joint tenancy does not make her his mother, and Isobell Gray’s widowhood does not prove her maternity. The girls’ already-proved father links remain proved. No identity merge, new original inspection, live WikiTree save or confidence upgrade is made.

evidence.label: John’s testament dative, CC9/7/27, register pp.478–480
Original family passage and qualified reading

chapters.title: Agnes Glasgow: a working daughter of James younger
body: Select James Glasgow younger (Glasgow-3921), the Corsankell tenant, as Agnes’s uncertain working father. Her probable 1601 and compatible 1606 Milneburne sasines and her 1628 Stevenston testament place her in the same small parish as the documented Corsankell family of 1559–1571. James younger’s approximate 1540 generation is a natural fit for the father of a woman already married by 1601. His existing plausible daughters Katherine Glasgow-1495 and Geillis Glasgow-3179 belong to the neighbouring Stevenston–Ardrossan women’s network; Geillis’s 1603 estate also names a James Glasgow in Stevenston in its debts. These are local family comparisons, not proved sisters or identification of the creditor. The earlier James-1168/Margaret Smith placement mixed two generations: Margaret is associated with the younger James, not the elder. Selecting the younger James gives the leading generational placement without inheriting that unsupported mother.

No record names Agnes’s father. Parish, generation and the existing family comparisons support only a low-confidence choice. The 1601 entry is a land-record registration, not a marriage date or an age statement; Agnes may already have been married for many years. As an illustration only, a married woman aged about 20–35 in 1601 would have been born about 1566–1581, making James younger about 26–41 and James elder about 51–66 at her birth. These are comparison assumptions, not birth estimates or exclusions. James elder remains an alternative father if Agnes was older. Edward Glasgow-1557 or another local Glasgow remains an alternative, especially if the unproved sisterhood with Jonet Glasgow-1494 is established. Edward’s own approximate 1570 birth makes that father generation less comfortable for a woman already married in 1601, but the estimate is not a hard conflict.

Neither the two women’s sisterhood nor the two Logan husbands’ brotherhood is documented. Under the selected James-younger father and the existing uncertain James → Edward → Jonet chain, Agnes could instead be Jonet’s aunt; that is a conditional model consequence, not a new proved kinship. Margaret Smith is not selected as Agnes’s mother, and her 1632 husband is not proved identical to the Corsankell man. The unnamed Stevenston elder of 1613 remains unidentified. No identity merge or live relationship edit is made.

Agnes’s captured WikiTree birth field is blank. The public c.1610 display was an unsupported inherited estimate and cannot date a woman probably already married in 1601. Her actual birth remains unknown; “before 1601” is a conditional outer boundary from the probable sasine identity. The 1628 testament date is not an exact death date. Stevenston is in Ayrshire; the corrected death locality is an uncertain inference from her stated residence, not a recorded place of death.

One uncertain father joins an existing family. The 1601 year denotes a probable record identity, not a birthday. Measured cohort memberships, the fixed baseline and confident links are preserved; only working connectivity gains the selected edge.

chapters.title: Marion is Ninian’s sister: Robert is their father
body: Ninian’s 1613 testament calls Marioun Glasgow his sister. The 1596 burgess roll names Ninian as Robert Glasgow’s second son. The combined statements, shared surname and compatible chronology support Robert as Marion’s confidently inferred father. This was already the approved conclusion on 28 September 2026; the current correction retires an erroneous Ninian-as-father rendering and restores the documented sibling role. No new record or certainty upgrade is claimed.

Robert’s fatherhood is an inference from the combined records, not an express father–daughter clause. Marion’s mother remains unidentified; the existing uncertain Jonet Meik attachment is retained without upgrading it. Her before-1592 birth is a boundary, not a recorded birthday. The separate Andrew-of-Corsoun daughter and Fultoun household questions remain as previously assessed.

The older table combined two different family roles. Its proved sibling finding was incorrectly rendered as a proved father link alongside the already supported Robert attachment. Both parent edges were consequently omitted from paternal connectivity as a conflict. The correction restores one existing supported connection; it does not add a generation, a new record or a new WikiTree update. Confident measurements change only because the existing approved Robert link is now included; the fixed baseline remains unchanged.

chapters.title: Agnes, Thomas and Marione: the Inveresk father links
body: The Inveresk children belong to the existing Thomas Glasgow and Agnes Thomsone household. Thomas and Marione’s indexed entries name that parent pair; Agnes’s entry names Thomas only. William Glasgow-2462’s inspected Findmypast transcript supplies the same parents in Inveresk in 1639. The children’s captured father ID, Glasgow-2459, is explicitly redirected to Glasgow-1103 in the saved WikiTree change data, and Thomas-1103’s captured family already includes them. Restoring the canonical father reconnects this existing household rather than discovering three new fathers.

The record-defined Inveresk father is Thomas Glasgow, but his identification with the combined Glasgow-1103 profile remains uncertain. That profile also represents the Glasgow child baptised in 1612 and the Linlithgow father associated with Hellin Bryse. A 1612 birth allows ages about 22, 25 and 30 at the Inveresk baptisms, but does not prove that adult identity. The profile’s estimated 1639 Bryse marriage overlaps the Agnes Thomsone household, which continues to December 1642. A later remarriage could fit the 1644 Bryse child, but is not established; a distinct Inveresk Thomas remains an alternative. Jannet’s 1640 Linlithgow entry names no mother. Keep these households distinguishable and do not infer a death or remarriage date.

No mother status is changed. Agnes’s index omits her mother; the existing Agnes Thomsone attachment is retained without upgrading it. Marione’s 13 December birth and 18 December christening remain separate. James Glasgow-3077’s naming-pattern placement is not documentary sibling proof. Margaret Glasgow-3050 has a conflicting William Glasgow/Bessie Howie index identification and is not used to support this reconstruction. The Weir husband is a separate comparison. No identity merge or live WikiTree change is performed.

Three formerly isolated public profile entries rejoin an existing household. This repairs merged-ID resolution and records its identity uncertainty; it is not three newly discovered parent relationships. Confident measurements and the fixed cohort are unchanged.

chapters.title: One working John across Glasgow and Stirling
body: Select the Glasgow burgess of 1447–1455 and the Stirling witness of 1475–1479/80 as the same man, at low confidence. Both groups use compatible John de Glasgu/Glasgw name forms in burgh-property witnessing, and the August 1475 catalogue places the Stirling John among burgesses. An adult active in 1447 could still witness in 1480 in his fifties or older. The conventional circa-1450 Stirling birth was inferred from an assumed young adult in 1475; it cannot establish a second man. A single compatible civic career is the simpler working model than inserting another generation from that estimate.

No shared holding, relative, trade, personal seal or distinctive repeated associate joins the cities. The Glasgow-to-Stirling change is not itself evidence of migration. Father–son, other kin and two unrelated namesakes remain viable alternatives. The name may still be a personal byname; this selection does not prove hereditary surname transmission. The two Glasgow acts remain one high-confidence group and the three Stirling acts another; only their cross-group identity is selected uncertain. No birth, death or additional parent is inferred.

The selected uncertain father links to Saltmarket candidate Glasgow-1095 and Alan Glasgow-3023 remain unchanged. Glasgow-1095 is still only a provisional Saltmarket representative: if it instead represents the older witness, that father link collapses as a duplicate identity. The earlier Malcolm father candidate remains unselected. Identity and father–son alternatives between the Glasgow and Stirling groups are not combined.

This joins two existing documentary record groups in the actual local model. Their accounts and within-group evidence grades remain intact. The earliest record of the named working ancestor changes from 1475 to 1447, while birth and death remain unknown. Five previously known occurrences are combined under one uncertain identity. The existing selected father hypotheses are unchanged, and no profile-component credit is claimed.

chapters.title: Margaret and Barbara: working daughters of Ninian Glasgow
body: Select daughter from the existing daughter-or-niece comparison with Ninian Glasgow. Margaret married Edinburgh cordiner William Hardie in 1611. Barbara Glasgow married another Edinburgh cordiner in 1616, while Ninian’s documented Glasgow son Robert is probably the cordiner admitted in 1613. Ninian’s possible son William supplies a family route into South Leith. Margaret’s estimated adult generation fits Ninian’s approximate 1550 generation. Together the generation, adjoining Edinburgh–Leith setting and repeated family craft make Ninian’s household the leading existing placement; daughter supplies the simplest provisional degree.

No record names Margaret’s father or proves that she and Barbara were sisters. Niece, another close relative or another local Glasgow family remain alternatives. The cordiners worked in different burghs; a shared trade does not prove one incorporation or apprenticeship. The Robert-cordiner identity and William’s Ninian parentage are supporting inferences. Margaret’s before-1595 birth is an adult-status estimate, not a baptism. Repeated William Hardie marriages do not prove one serial husband or Margaret’s death. No mother is selected.

Select Ninian Glasgow as an uncertain working father within Barbara’s already preferred household or immediate collateral circle. Barbara married Edinburgh cordiner George Johnstoun in 1616; Ninian’s documented Glasgow son Robert is probably the cordiner admitted in 1613, and possible son William lived at South Leith. Barbara’s adult generation fits Ninian’s family. Her possible identity with Barbara Glasgow-3182, the 1611 South Leith bride already tentatively placed as Ninian’s daughter, supplies a second, explicitly conditional route to the same father.

No record names Barbara’s father. Daughter is selected provisionally over niece or another family; trade alone cannot decide the degree. The Glasgow and Edinburgh cordiners are not shown to share an incorporation. Barbara-3302, Barbara-3182 and Barbara-567 remain separate profiles with unresolved possible identity links. If the 1611 and 1616 brides are one woman, these two Ninian attachments describe one possible daughter twice, not two historical sisters. If the Little mother Barbara-567 is the same woman, her existing William Glasgow-3522 father claim is a competing explanation. The disputed Wilson entry, widowhood and remarriage sequence remain unresolved. No mother or identity merge is selected.

Two previously parentless imported profile entries join Ninian’s branch. The measure counts profiles, not deduplicated historical people: Barbara may be the same woman as the already linked Barbara-3182. This selection is no evidence of two sisters or a confirmed father. Confident links and the fixed baseline stay unchanged.

evidence.label: Barbara: complete evidence and identity alternatives

chapters.title: Stirling John as a working father of Saltmarket John and Alan
body: Select John Glasgw of Stirling as the uncertain father of Saltmarket John, using Glasgow-1095 as a provisional Saltmarket representative. Stirling John was an adult witness by 1475 and a burgess in the August charter description. That fits an older generation than the Saltmarket owner, securely recorded in 1527 and conditionally associated with the adult alias-Smith purchaser in 1506. The uncommon name, consecutive civic-property settings and the weak Brady/Brade surname-network clue support the existing leading father hypothesis. The Saltmarket parcel passing to William by 1528/29 favours placing this candidate with William’s family.

The imported profile is a conflated placeholder whose biography also points to the Stirling witness. It is not proved to be Saltmarket John. If it instead represents the Stirling man, this proposed father link collapses as an identity duplicate. The 1506 alias-Smith identity and circa-1480 birth are conditional; no kinship clause or shared holding joins Stirling to Saltmarket. Brother, cousin, other predecessor or unrelated namesake remain alternatives. The later 15 October review selects the 1447–1455 Glasgow burgess and Stirling witness as one uncertain working identity. Father–son and other-family alternatives remain unselected; the two documentary groups stay separately inspectable.

Select son, at low confidence, from the existing son/brother/nephew comparison with John Glasgw of Stirling. John’s adult activity in 1475–1480 is compatible with fathering a man killed before the 1494/95 proceeding. The rare surname in the same late-fifteenth-century record horizon makes this named household a useful provisional placement; no invented intermediary is needed. The father choice supplies a revisable one-generation model, rather than claiming that the court record names John.

No age, home, occupation or relative is named for Alan. Brother, nephew or another early family remain viable, and the father choice is weaker than the Saltmarket hypothesis. Jedburgh is the court venue, not Alan’s residence or death place; Pilmure’s Ednem association and Ker’s surety do not supply Alan’s kin. The printed 1494/95 year and regnal-year discrepancy await manuscript collation. No mother, wife, child, exact birth or exact death is inferred.

These are two selected uncertain father links and no certainty upgrades. John is a named, source-defined person with a full public account; birth and death remain unknown. He acts as an uncounted connector between existing profiles, so the profile denominator and confident graph stay unchanged. The later review selects one uncertain Glasgow–Stirling identity; a father–son relationship remains an unselected alternative.

chapters.title: Three more early family placements, explicitly uncertain
body: The local working tree now selects William of Saltmarket as Michael of Stevenston’s possible father, Andrew of Calder as Jonat Menzeis’s possible father, and Ninian as Barbara Wilson’s possible father. These choices use the existing brother/cousin, same-parish remarriage and daughter/niece comparisons.

Michael Glasgow of Stevenston: The existing Stevenston study places Michael as a probable brother or cousin of James elder of Corsankell, rather than his son. Michael was an adult witness in the Glencairn estate network in 1549; both appear in the same small estate landscape in the 1559–60 teind list. Their approximate 1525 and 1515 generations fit brothers. Select the brother option provisionally and extend James’s already uncertain father William to Michael. This uses an existing older household without inventing an intervening person. The Mathie–Glencairn network supplies a credible route between the burgh family and these estates. Limits: The brother-versus-cousin choice is unresolved, and James’s own father William is uncertain. No record calls Michael William’s son. A cousin through another burgh household, an older generation than the estimated 1525 birth, or a separate family remains possible. Brakpleuch and Dubbs may represent one Michael or two. No mother, exact birth or death is inferred.

Jonat Glasgow, wife of David Menzeis: Jonat is the mother in a Mid Calder baptism in 1609. The existing comparison prefers her possible identity with Jonet Glasgow who married Martin Ramsy in the same parish in 1624, fifteen years later. That Jonet is already placed as Andrew’s testament daughter. Select Andrew as Jonat’s uncertain father through this local identity reconstruction. Her estimated 1585 generation fits Andrew’s household; the same name, parish and feasible remarriage sequence favour this model over the more distant Ninian household. Limits: This combines two uncertain identity steps: the 1609 mother with the 1624 bride, and the bride with Andrew’s testament daughter. David Menzeis’s death and the bride’s widowhood are not recorded in the material reviewed. Jonat and Jonet may be different women; retain both profiles and do not count an identity merge. Ninian Glasgow remains a competing father hypothesis. No mother is attached.

Barbara Glasgow, wife of Johne Wilsoune: The existing branch assessment already favours Barbara as a daughter or niece of Ninian. Her 1611 South Leith marriage entry fits the Leith setting of Ninian’s possible son William and the adjoining Edinburgh craft households; Ninian’s documented son Robert was a cordiner. The estimated 1590 daughter generation fits Ninian’s estimated 1550 generation. Select daughter as the simpler working placement within this already identified household, while retaining niece as an alternative. This is a combined locality, generation and family-network inference. Limits: Neither the marriage entry nor Ninian’s testament names Barbara as his daughter. The proposed Leith brother William is himself uncertain, and shared craft geography is suggestive rather than individual proof. Barbara may instead be Ninian’s niece or belong to another local family. If she is Barbara-567, the existing William-3522 father claim becomes a rival explanation. The adult Barbara identities remain separate, the 1611 date discrepancy stays open, and no mother is assigned.

Each is low confidence and counts only as a selected uncertain parent in the working graph. Keep possible duplicate profiles separate, mothers independent, and the confident graph unchanged. No new source reading is claimed.

chapters.title: Four selected working connections
body: The local working tree now selects Andrew of Calder as tentative father of James, John of Linlithgow and David of Mid Calder. It selects the older Mid Calder/Quothquan John as tentative father of the1640s Kirknewton John. These are logical reconstructions from material already on this site, not newly discovered parentage records.

James Glasgow → Andrew Glasgow of Calder: Andrew’s documented rural Calder household is the preferred working anchor for James’s nearby Mid Calder family. He was alive across the estimated1575–1586 birth interval of all three Lothian fathers; Hermand John’s1577 death would require an earlier birth estimate for David. That favours this coherent provisional family without excluding the other father. Andrew was alive until1598 and the uncertain generations allow James to be an older son. This uses the actual Calder setting and compatible family sequence, not the withdrawn assertion that the testament named James. James’s Inveresk/Fisherrow identity remains a separate uncertainty. Alternatives: John of Hermand-3181 is another plausible older local father. The George named at Mureistoun1586 and the George witness1605 are a competing father/relative lead; identifying that George with merchant1099 would require additional identity assumptions and young fatherhood. None is excluded. Andrew’s omission of James weakens this model; it does not disprove an older son.

John Glasgow of Linlithgow → Andrew Glasgow of Calder: Select the same older Calder household as the working origin for this neighbouring Lothian family. John’s estimated1579 generation and children recorded1613–1622 fit an older son of Andrew, whose own father is tentatively John-1093. The proximity and compatible generations make this a useful shared-family model alongside James and David, rather than an assertion that the three are proved brothers. Alternatives: John of Hermand-3181 is a compatible alternative if John1561’s estimated birth is earlier than1577. A separate unnamed local father remains possible. Andrew’s1598 testament does not name John; do not restore the obsolete James/Andrew/William child list or attach Jonet Anderson as mother.

David Glasgow of Mid Calder → Andrew Glasgow of Calder: David’s1606 and1612 Mid Calder baptisms place his household in the same small Calder area as the earlier Andrew household. His approximate generation permits Andrew to be his father. The first recorded daughter Elspeth is consistent with the Elizat name in Andrew’s household, a minor naming clue rather than a mother identification. Select Andrew as the tentative shared father with James and John; exact birth years remain estimates. Alternatives: John of Hermand-3181 or another older local Glasgow could be the father. If David’s approximate1586 birth were established, he would have been young when omitted from Andrew’s1598 testament, making that omission more troublesome. It is not an established birth date. Elizat Stevinsoun and the discredited Jonet Anderson attribution are not automatically assigned as mothers.

John Glasgow of Kirknewton → John Glasgow, Mid Calder/Quothquan working identity: The older John already represents the father named in Mid Calder baptisms1608–1609. His son John-1086, baptised1608, is a viable earlier identity for the adult John who had children in neighbouring Kirknewton/East Calder1646–1650: age38 at the1646 birth is straightforward. Select the older John as working father of3610 on that local and chronological reconstruction. Keep the two son profiles separate while testing their possible identity. Alternatives: John-1086 has a later Biggar account that has not been equated with3610. They may be different men, and the older father’s Mid Calder/Montfoid/Quothquan identity is itself uncertain. Robert-4006 is another generationally compatible Calder father. This does not restore the former unsupported William-1087 father or treat1629 as a recorded birthday.
All four edges are uncertain and count only in the working pedigree. Confident relationships, raw WikiTree parent fields and the fixed cohort are unchanged. No mother is assigned by these selections.

chapters.title: Murieston: an earlier George beside James’s household
body: The original Mid Calder baptism of 17 February 1605 names father James Glasgow, provisionally in Muirestoun, and adult witness George Glasgow. The 1586 Calder muster list names George Glasgw in Mureistoun. Murieston is the probable common locality; the two older George occurrences may be one man, but no kinship is stated.

The 19-year interval permits one adult George in both records. A father-of-James hypothesis is possible, alongside uncle, brother or neighbour; no pedigree edge or certainty upgrade is counted. James-991 remains the compatible father anchor, while the Inveresk/Fisherrow identity question is separate.

Compare the other Mid Calder baptism pages for the same holding and witnesses, then inspect NLS MS.3724 and Beveridge’s transcript MS.3725 for George, James, heirs, leases and succession at Mureistoun. The catalogue places the 1586 land-title courts at original pp.1–15 and the chronological court sequence at pp.23–189; it records a gap between 2 May 1592 and 26 November 1594. These manuscript pages have not been read.

chapters.title: Record limits behind the working parent selections
body: John Glasgow is the father named at Linlithgow baptisms in 1613, 1617 and 1622; David is named at Mid Calder baptisms in 1606 and 1612. Their live parent fields are empty, as checked 15 October 2026, while biography prose still repeats the superseded Andrew/Jonet testament rationale. Complete local amendments retain the sources and wider family hypotheses.

John’s proposed child Thomas, indexed in Glasgow in 1612, has recorded father George Glasgow and mother Margaret Steuart. This is a conflict for the record-defined child; later adult Thomas identities remain a separate question.

The former John-3608 now resolves to John-3296. His associated Mid Calder 1608/1609 father entries and the Linlithgow sequence are compatible, but no shared wife, occupation, holding or cross-parish identity is established. Original parish pages and named heirs are the next connection test. No paternal join or certainty upgrade is counted.
These limits remain in force. The local working model now selects Andrew3163 as uncertain father of John and David, rather than leaving the compatible branches unplaced; no parent is newly proved.

body: The ancestry programme now measures separate paternal components, unattached fathers with at least two children, the largest branch and connected pairs. Confidently marked and working links are reported separately, with a fixed initial cohort for progress comparisons.

chapters.title: Medieval and early-burgh occurrences
body: Medieval officeholders, messengers, clerics and burgh entries preserve name occurrences across several places and roles.
A shared surname, an office phrase or a similar John does not itself establish one person or a descent line; pre-1500 subjects remain documentary research destinations.

The official description of the 8 August 1475 Stirling charter, B66/25/43, groups John Glesgw among the burgess witnesses. Three Stirling occurrences are now assigned to the same working identity. This strengthens the civic comparison with the Glasgow burgess of 1447–1455; one career across 1447–1480 is viable, and an estimated circa-1450 birth cannot establish a separate son. Parent–child or other kinship remains an alternative. Saltmarket activity is secure in 1527; the 1506 alias-Smith identification remains possible.

The working model now selects the 1447–1455 Glasgow burgess and 1475–1480 Stirling John as one uncertain identity. Both documentary groups remain intact; the father–son alternative is not also selected. The named working ancestor therefore reaches back to 1447, with no new parent edge or profile-component credit.

chapters.title: Quothquan tenants before the later weaver
body: The full Carnwath court book is publicly readable. Printed passages name Robert and William Glesquho in 1524, John as a Quothquan tenant in 1525/26 and Upper Quothquan in 1531/32, and Thomas Gleschow at Quothquan in 1527/28. John’s later records include a forfeiture decree and an October 1532 malt case.

John and Thomas form a possible early local family group to connect with James Glasgow, the Quothquan weaver documented in 1607–1612 and dead by 1624. No father, spouse or child is named for the early men in the inspected passages. The missing generations remain an explicit research question; the burgh candidates are retained.

Court headings can have wrong years or repeat an event. Dates here follow Dickinson’s cautious Appendix B, including February 1527/28 and the bracketed 1525/26 year. This corrects the former search-only access note; no new paternal join is counted.

The remaining indexed name-bearing passages are now read: Thomas’s repeated entries consolidate into five court meetings, with a March 1528 judgment concerning cultivation and rent prohibitions. No named Glasgow kin or individual tenancy transfer was recovered. The next test is leases and named heirs. The separate Torphichen “Wilyame Glasgow” lead is an index-boundary false hit: Kamis, Wilyame precedes Glasgow the place.

body: Protocols, burgess admissions and testaments permit especially careful reconstruction in the Glasgow burgh, including one expressly named parent–child generation.

chapters.title: Ayrshire estates, households and ministry
body: Teind lists, charters, sasines and parish material document people at Corsankell, Stevenston, Kilwinning and Kilbirnie.
Some records explicitly define a household; estate proximity, later local tradition and same-name candidates remain research leads until a record states the bridge.

chapters.title: Calder and Lothian testaments and registers
body: Testaments at Hirmenschelis and Corstoun name small households, while baptism indexes provide two sequences for a father called James Glasgow.
The records correct earlier inherited claims, but they do not identify every child with a modern profile or settle whether the James sequences represent one household.

chapters.title: Findmypast follow-up: indexed records and open originals (15 October 2026)
body: The focused follow-up authenticated William Glascoe's 10 July 1610 South Leith marriage to Catherine Fraith/Fraser and records a new Haddington household: Issobell Glasgow, born 24 and baptised 26 November 1639, daughter of William Glasgow and Issobella Miral.

Crossle's 9 December 1639 abstract names an Archbold Glascow clerk; the duplicate transcript IDs are retained, but the original document 849 has not been inspected, so identification with Archibald Glasgow-1101 remains probable. Walter's 1647/1649 and Margaret's 1649/1646 competing indexes require original-page checks.

Visually checked SRO Indexes 38 pp.187–188 name Alexander as son of James, the Fisherrow tailor and Musselburgh burgess; Christina Bye is James’s spouse and Janet Clerk is Alexander’s. Indexes 44 pp.159–160 repeatedly associate Alexander with James, weaver: 14 February 1646 (33/258), 15 May 1646 (33/360), 10 February 1647 (34/287). Edward shares the first 1646 reference. The earlier June 1646 attribution belongs to Isobel Givan in the preceding row. These are registration dates; original instruments remain unread.

James the weaver could be the older James, Alexander’s son James-3923, the Edinburgh weaver James-1150, or another man. Eduard-994, indexed in Inveresk in 1609 with father James, is an alternative to Edwards 1557 and 1558. A match could explain the association within the proposed Fisherrow household. The possible Corsankell bridge and exact kinship remain open; this batch adds no paternal join.
The 1623 Robert Glasgow tanner and 1625 town-officer references remain separate identity questions.
